Anal sex, a workbook

Project 67 · a workbook, kind workbook, on the anal sex report · index · repo randomcase/anal-sex-a-workbook

ten pages, until we understand the numbers; each page a lesson, exercises, and the answers folded under them

A workbook is not a report. The report states; the workbook asks. Ten pages, each one a thing you must be able to do before turning it — count, compute, classify, explain, date — and the answers folded under the questions, because a workbook you cannot check is a claim. Every figure is from project 66 and has a source there.

Page 1 of 10 — Scale

About 36% of American women and 42% of American men aged 18–44 have had anal sex with an opposite-sex partner (NSFG 2011–13). About 4–5% of most-recent sexual events included it (NSSHB 2009). In Britain about one in six adults under 45 did it in the past year (Natsal-3). The lifetime figure roughly doubled between 1992 and 2009. Numbers like these mean nothing until they are set against each other.

Exercises

  1. Forty percent of adults have ever done it; five percent of events include it. What does the gap between those two numbers tell you about how often the people who have tried it repeat it?
    answer

    That most who have tried it do it rarely. If 40% of adults produced 5% of all events, the average person who has tried it is doing it in about one event in eight, and since a minority of them account for most of the repeats, the median tryer has done it a few times in their life and stopped.

  2. One in six British adults did it in the past year, and about 40% have ever done it. What fraction of those who have ever done it did it this year?
    answer

    About 17 / 40, roughly 40%. Six in ten of the people who have tried it did not do it this year.

  3. The lifetime figure doubled between a 1992 face-to-face survey and a 2009 anonymous online one. Name two explanations and say what evidence would separate them.
    answer

    Behaviour changed, or people answered more honestly when no one was in the room. A survey that ran both modes on the same population in the same year would separate them; the ones that have done so for other sexual questions find the mode effect real but smaller than a doubling, so probably both.

  4. The health literature on this act is almost entirely about men who have sex with men. Using the prevalence figures, say who does most of the anal sex in the United States.
    answer

    Heterosexual couples, by a wide margin. About 3–4% of men are gay or bisexual; 85–90% of them do it, so roughly 3% of men. About 42% of all men do it with women. The heterosexual count is more than ten times larger; the literature is about the group where the per-act risk and the epidemic met.

Page 2 of 10 — The passage

The anal canal is 3–4 cm long and closed by two rings: an internal sphincter that is involuntary and an external one under conscious control. The rectum beyond it is 12–15 cm, lined by a single layer of cells, and produces no lubricant. The prostate sits 5–7 cm in on the front wall.

Exercises

  1. Which of the two sphincters can a person relax on purpose, and what does the other one respond to?
    answer

    The external one. The internal sphincter responds to pressure and time, and clamps to pain and fear. This is why "relax" is useless advice and "slowly" is the mechanism.

  2. How far in is the prostate, and how far in is the far end of the rectum? Draw the passage to scale on a line 18 cm long.
    answer

    Prostate at 5–7 cm; rectum ends at roughly 16–19 cm from the outside. On an 18 cm line the canal is the first 3–4 cm, the prostate sits just past it, and most of the length is rectum. Anything longer than about 18 cm is reaching the sigmoid colon.

  3. The vagina has a many-layered lining and lubricates; the rectum has a single layer and does not. Name the two consequences that follow directly.
    answer

    Tearing without added lubricant, and a thinner barrier to infection. Both feed page 3.

Page 3 of 10 — Per-act arithmetic

HIV transmissions per 10,000 exposures to an untreated HIV-positive partner (Patel et al. 2014): receptive anal 138, insertive anal 11, receptive vaginal 8, insertive vaginal 4. Per-act risks combine as P(at least one) = 1 − (1 − p)n if the acts are independent, which is roughly true.

Exercises

  1. How many times riskier is receptive anal than receptive vaginal sex, per act?
    answer

    138 / 8 ≈ 17 times.

  2. A person has receptive anal sex 100 times with an untreated HIV-positive partner. What is the probability of acquiring HIV?
    answer

    1 − (1 − 0.0138)100 = 1 − 0.9862100 ≈ 1 − 0.249 ≈ 75%.

  3. Same question for receptive vaginal sex, 100 times.
    answer

    1 − 0.9992100 ≈ 1 − 0.923 ≈ 7.7%. Ten times as many acts as it takes anal sex to reach the same probability.

  4. Why is "1.38% per act" a misleading way to read a 138-per-10,000 figure for a person in a relationship?
    answer

    Because nobody has one act. Over a year of a relationship the per-act figure compounds into the majority probability in exercise 2. The per-act number is for comparing acts; the compound number is for deciding.

  5. The partner's status in these figures is "untreated HIV-positive". A stranger's status is unknown. What number do you need, and what is it in the United States?
    answer

    The prevalence of untreated, unsuppressed HIV in the partner pool. US adult HIV prevalence is about 0.4%; among men who have sex with men roughly 10–15%, of whom a third or so are not suppressed. Multiply the per-act risk by that fraction before compounding.

Page 4 of 10 — Stacking protections

Against a baseline of 138 per 10,000 receptive acts: consistent condom use removes about 70%; PrEP taken as prescribed removes about 99%; a partner with a suppressed viral load has transmitted zero times in about 77,000 observed condomless acts. Reductions multiply: what is left after two independent protections is (1 − a)(1 − b) of the baseline.

Exercises

  1. What is left of 138 after condoms alone? After PrEP alone? After both?
    answer

    Condoms: 138 × 0.30 ≈ 41. PrEP: 138 × 0.01 ≈ 1.4. Both: 138 × 0.30 × 0.01 ≈ 0.4 per 10,000 acts.

  2. Redo page 3, exercise 2 (100 acts) for a person on PrEP.
    answer

    1 − (1 − 0.000138)100 ≈ 1.4%, down from 75%.

  3. Condoms are usually quoted at 80–95% for vaginal sex. Why is the anal figure lower?
    answer

    Breakage and slippage are more common during anal sex, and the "consistent use" studies still include acts where the condom failed. The 70% is condoms as used, not condoms as designed.

  4. The PARTNER studies observed zero transmissions in 77,000 acts. Does that prove the risk is zero? What is the upper bound?
    answer

    It cannot prove zero; it puts a ceiling on it. With zero events in 77,000 acts, the 95% upper bound is about 3 / 77,000, or 0.4 per 10,000 acts, and the estimate is lower still because most of those acts were vaginal. For practical purposes the guidance says "zero", and the arithmetic says "below anything else on this page".

  5. Rank the four protections by how much of the remaining risk they remove, and say which one depends least on the person at risk.
    answer

    Suppressed partner, PrEP, condoms, then everything on the lubricant and pace list. The suppressed partner is the one protection that does not depend on the person at risk doing anything; it depends on the other person being in care, which is page 9.

Page 5 of 10 — The other infections

Rectal gonorrhoea and chlamydia are usually symptomless, are found in about 10–20% of men who have sex with men at screening, and are missed by a urine test. Oral-anal contact carries hepatitis A, shigella and giardia. Syphilis, herpes, hepatitis B and mpox pass by the same route. Four vaccines apply: HPV, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, mpox.

Exercises

  1. A clinic tests urine only. Roughly what share of rectal gonorrhoea and chlamydia does it find?
    answer

    Very little. Most rectal infections occur without a urethral one; studies of men tested at all three sites find that urine-only testing would have missed 70–90% of the infections found.

  2. Which organisms on this page travel by oral-anal contact rather than by intercourse, and what protects against them?
    answer

    Hepatitis A, shigella, giardia, and the other gut organisms. Vaccination for hepatitis A; for the rest, barriers, washing, and not doing it during or just after a gut infection. The shigella outbreaks since 2010 were among men with no other risk than this.

  3. A rectal chlamydia infection has no symptoms. Why does it still matter for HIV?
    answer

    Inflammation recruits the immune cells HIV targets to the rectal lining and can break the surface. Rectal STIs multiply the per-act HIV risk on page 3 by roughly two to three, and are a marker that condomless receptive sex is occurring.

  4. Name the four vaccines and, for each, the age or group guidance in the United States.
    answer

    HPV: routine through 26, shared decision to 45. Hepatitis A and B: all adults not already immune, and specifically men who have sex with men. Mpox: two doses for people with exposures or in the risk groups defined in the 2022–23 outbreak.

Page 6 of 10 — HPV and the ANCHOR trial

Anal cancer runs at about 2 per 100,000 a year in the general population and about 85 per 100,000 among HIV-positive men who have sex with men. The ANCHOR trial (2022) randomised 4,459 such men with high-grade precursor lesions to treatment or monitoring; treatment cut progression to cancer by 57%.

Exercises

  1. How many times the general rate is the HIV-positive MSM rate?
    answer

    85 / 2 ≈ 42 times. Comparable to cervical cancer before screening, which is why the trial was run.

  2. A cohort of 10,000 HIV-positive men who have sex with men is followed for ten years. How many anal cancers do you expect without intervention? With ANCHOR-style treatment of the precursors?
    answer

    Without: 85 per 100,000 per year × 10,000 × 10 = 85 cancers. With treatment of the lesions: 85 × 0.43 ≈ 37, so about 48 avoided. The trial's own cancers were fewer because follow-up was shorter.

  3. The HPV vaccine given before exposure prevents the infection that causes nearly all anal cancer. Why does the report call it the only intervention that works "at the source", and why does it not help most of the men in the trial?
    answer

    Because everything else, screening, treating lesions, treating cancer, acts after the virus is established. It does not help most men in the trial because they were exposed decades before the vaccine existed; the vaccine is for the cohort behind them.

Page 7 of 10 — Pain

At their most recent act, 72% of women reported pain during receptive anal intercourse, 15% of men did, and 30% of women reported pain during vaginal intercourse (Herbenick et al. 2015). A qualitative study of English 16–18-year-olds found young women expecting it to hurt, young men expecting to persuade, and both treating pain as normal.

Exercises

  1. What is the gap between the women's and men's receptive figures, in points and as a ratio?
    answer

    57 points; 72 / 15 ≈ 4.8 times.

  2. Give three reasons the men's figure is lower that have nothing to do with anatomy.
    answer

    Practice: men who have receptive anal sex tend to have had more of it. Preparation: more likely to use lubricant, and enough of it. Power: more likely to be in a setting where stopping is easy and expected. Anatomy differs little between the sexes at the anus; the difference is in the rooms.

  3. Page 2 says the internal sphincter clamps to pain and fear. Use that to explain why "it always hurts at first" is both true and wrong.
    answer

    True because an act begun before the internal sphincter has relaxed will hurt; wrong because the hurt is the sphincter resisting, which is a signal to stop and wait, not a phase to push through. Pushing through it tightens the muscle further and tears the lining.

  4. The English study is qualitative: about forty interviews, no percentages. What can it tell you that the 72% cannot, and what can it not tell you?
    answer

    It can tell you why: the expectations on both sides, and how the pain was talked about. It cannot tell you how common those expectations are. The two studies are the two halves of one finding.

Page 8 of 10 — Douching and lubricant

Body fluids sit at about 290 mOsm/kg. The WHO advisory (2012) recommends lubricants under about 1,200 mOsm/kg; many glycerin-based products run 2,000–10,000 and strip the rectal lining in the laboratory. Nonoxynol-9 damages rectal tissue. About half to two-thirds of men who have sex with men douche before receptive sex; a meta-analysis of 24 studies found douchers with 2.8 times the odds of HIV and 2.4 times the odds of a rectal STI.

Exercises

  1. How many times more concentrated than body fluid is a 10,000 mOsm/kg lubricant? What does that do to the cells it touches?
    answer

    About 34 times. Water leaves the cells to dilute it; the single-layer lining shrinks, lifts, and sheds, which is what the colonoscopy studies photographed within an hour of application.

  2. Sort: water-based glycerin lubricant, silicone lubricant, coconut oil, saliva, a nonoxynol-9 spermicidal gel. Which are safe with a latex condom, which are safe for the rectum, which are neither?
    answer

    Silicone: safe for both. Water-based: safe with latex; safe for the rectum only if its osmolality is low, which the label rarely says. Coconut oil: safe for tissue, destroys latex. Saliva: safe with latex, too thin to prevent tearing, and a route for gonorrhoea. Nonoxynol-9: neither; it damages rectal tissue and is not recommended there.

  3. The douching odds ratio is 2.8. Give three explanations and say why the 2.8 is an upper bound on the one that matters.
    answer

    Douching damages the lining; douching disturbs the rectal microbiome; men who douche have more receptive partners. The studies are mostly cross-sectional and cannot fully adjust for the third, so some of the 2.8 is who douches, not what douching does. The causal share is smaller than 2.8 and is not known.

  4. Write the douching guidance that follows from the evidence in one sentence.
    answer

    If at all: plain water or isotonic saline, body temperature, small volume, once, well before, no soap, no commercial hyperosmolar enema, no repeat.

Page 9 of 10 — Projections, and assault

The US Ending the HIV Epidemic initiative (2019) set a 75% cut in new infections by 2025 and 90% by 2030 from a 2018 baseline of about 36,000. The 2022 estimate was about 32,000. UNAIDS set 370,000 new infections worldwide by 2025; the 2024 estimate was about 1.3 million, down from 2.1 million in 2010. Rape does not appear in any HIV surveillance category; the report estimates its share by arithmetic.

Exercises

  1. What percentage fall did the United States achieve from 2018 to 2022, and what was the 2025 target in numbers? By what factor will the target be missed if 2025 looks like 2022?
    answer

    (36 − 32) / 36 ≈ 12%. Target: 36,000 × 0.25 ≈ 9,000. Miss: 32,000 / 9,000 ≈ 3.5 times.

  2. Worldwide, what share of the planned 2010–2025 reduction was achieved by 2024?
    answer

    Planned: 2.1 → 0.37 million, a fall of 1.73 million (82%). Achieved: 2.1 → 1.3, a fall of 0.8 million (38%). About 0.8 / 1.73 ≈ 46% of the planned reduction, in 14 of the 15 years.

  3. The trials on page 4 held: PrEP and treatment work as promised. Where, then, is the gap between projection and record?
    answer

    In coverage, not efficacy. About 40% of US infections come from people undiagnosed and 40% from people diagnosed but not in care; PrEP reached 36% of those with an indication against a 50% target, unevenly by race and region. The per-act numbers did not change; the number of acts under protection did not change enough.

  4. Estimate the share of US HIV infections attributable to rape. Use 450,000 rapes and sexual assaults a year (NCVS), a per-assault transmission risk of 0.1–0.5%, and an assailant HIV prevalence of 0.4–4%. Compare to 32,000 new infections.
    answer

    Low: 450,000 × 0.001 × 0.004 ≈ 2. High: 450,000 × 0.005 × 0.04 ≈ 90. Against 32,000 that is 0.006% to 0.3%. Even the high case is under one in three hundred. The claim that assault explains most or all HIV among any group is off by two to three orders of magnitude.

  5. Gay and bisexual men report lifetime sexual violence at about 40–47%, heterosexual men at 21%, heterosexual women at 43%. What does this say about the claim that every gay man who acquires HIV was raped?
    answer

    That it is false twice over: a minority of gay men report ever being raped (reviews give a median near 30% for any sexual assault, lower for rape), and the exercise above shows assault cannot produce more than a small fraction of infections in any group. Most HIV among men who have sex with men comes from consensual receptive sex with a partner whose status was unknown, by the arithmetic of page 3.

  6. Where does violence matter statistically for HIV, and by how much?
    answer

    Intimate-partner violence against women in high-prevalence settings. The South African cohort found 1.5 times the incidence among women reporting it, and attributed about one in eight new infections in the cohort to it. That is a multiplier on the consensual route, not a separate route.

Page 10 of 10 — The law, by case

England made the act capital in 1533 and hanged the last two men for it in 1835; the death penalty went in 1861, the offence in private in 1967, the last exception in 2004. The Indian Penal Code's section 377 (1860) carried the offence to every British colony. Illinois repealed in 1961; Lawrence v Texas struck the last thirteen US laws in 2003; Navtej Singh Johar struck 377 in India in 2018. About 64 jurisdictions still criminalise it; Trinidad's appeal court put its law back in 2025.

Exercises

  1. How many years was the act a capital offence in England? How many years from the last hanging to the end of the death penalty for it?
    answer

    1533 to 1861: 328 years. 1835 to 1861: 26 years during which the sentence was passed and commuted.

  2. Name the last two men hanged for it, the date, and who saw them in the cell.
    answer

    James Pratt and John Smith, Newgate, 27 November 1835. Charles Dickens visited the condemned cell and wrote about them in Sketches by Boz. Both were pardoned in 2017.

  3. The 1967 Act legalised the act for men over 21. List the steps to 16 with the case behind each.
    answer

    21 → 18: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994, after the Commons rejected 16 by 307 to 280. 18 → 16: Sutherland v United Kingdom (European Commission, 1997) found the difference discriminatory; the Lords blocked the bill twice; the Parliament Acts were invoked, and the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2000 took effect 8 January 2001. Thirty-four years from 21 to 16.

  4. Which case did Lawrence v Texas overrule, how many years apart were they, and what did the earlier case's author later say?
    answer

    Bowers v Hardwick, 1986; seventeen years. Justice Powell, who cast the fifth vote to uphold Georgia's law, said in 1990 that he had "probably made a mistake".

  5. Name the Indian cases in order, with the court and the result of each.
    answer

    Queen-Empress v Khairati, Allahabad High Court 1884: first reported prosecution, conviction quashed. Naz Foundation, Delhi High Court 2009: section read down. Koushal, Supreme Court 2013: restored. Navtej Singh Johar, Supreme Court 2018: struck, unanimously.

  6. Three Caribbean courts struck their laws in 2022. Name the countries and the claimants. Then say what happened in Trinidad and Tobago in 2025 and why.
    answer

    Antigua and Barbuda (Orden David), St Kitts and Nevis (Jamal Jeffers), Barbados (River and another). In Trinidad, the Court of Appeal on 25 March 2025 reversed Jones v Attorney General (2018) on the ground that the constitution's savings clause shields laws inherited from before independence, the same clause that defeated Maurice Tomlinson in Jamaica in 2023. An appeal to the Privy Council is filed.

  7. Which countries added a criminal law in 2024–2025, and which country's law lasted eleven months?
    answer

    Iraq (April 2024), Mali (November 2024), Burkina Faso (September 2025). Gabon criminalised in July 2019 and repealed in June 2020.

  8. Of the roughly 64 jurisdictions that criminalise the act, how many keep the death penalty on the books and in how many is it carried out or a live sentence? Name the latter.
    answer

    Twelve on the books; six in practice: Iran, Saudi Arabia, Yemen (thirteen sentences in Ibb, 2024), Afghanistan, parts of Somalia, and northern Nigeria by sentence though not by execution. The country table in the report has the rest.

Wanted: a page 11 on the economics — the cost of a course of PrEP against the lifetime cost of one infection, by country. The figures exist; they are not yet in the report.
